summary:
Artemis II Simulator is a free web app that recreates NASA's Artemis II crewed lunar flyby, from the launch pad to atmospheric entry about nine days later. It runs on a simplified physics model, so its figures are approximate and illustrative, not official mission data. The flight comes from physics, not a pre-animated path. The model uses real thrust and mass data from NASA's SLS and Orion guides, atmospheric drag, and the gravity of the Earth and the Moon. The Moon follows its real April 2026 orbit.

The screen pairs a conceptual Orion-style cockpit with a 2D mission map and a true-scale 3D view. The user flies the key maneuvers, and real consequences follow. A well-flown mission closely matches NASA's published timeline. Mistakes can end in a lunar impact or a failed reentry.

The goal is to make a real crewed lunar mission understandable through hands-on learning. Values are either computed by the model or taken from cited NASA sources. It is built with TypeScript, React and Three.js and runs entirely in the browser. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.
details:
What it does and how it works:

Artemis II Simulator is a web app that recreates NASA's Artemis II crewed lunar flyby, from the launch pad to atmospheric entry about nine days later. It uses a simplified physics model, so its figures are approximate and illustrative. Physics computes the whole flight: thrust, propellant use, changing mass, drag, and the gravity of the Earth and the Moon. Only the events that are also automated on the real vehicle are pre-programmed. On the left of the screen is a conceptual Orion-style cockpit with display pages, guarded switches, an autopilot, hand controllers, alarms and Mission Control messages. On the right are a 2D mission map, which can show the free-return "figure 8", and a true-scale 3D view. The user arms each crew burn. If it is late, wrong or skipped, physics decides the outcome.

Value it provides:

It shows why the mission flies the way it does, not just what happens. The user learns by doing and sees real consequences. Every number is computed by the model or cited to a NASA source, and assumptions are flagged. The results are checked against NASA's published timeline. For example, the translunar injection lands within one second of the published time.

Intended impact:

It aims to make a real crewed lunar mission understandable to students, educators and space enthusiasts, and to build intuition for orbital mechanics that static infographics can't give. All of it runs in a browser.

Tools used:

The app is written in TypeScript and React and built with Vite. Three.js draws the 2D map and the 3D view. Development was done with Claude Code, Anthropic's AI coding assistant. The app is deployed on GitHub Pages.

In what sense it is creative:

It is a playable model: the same physics produces both the nominal mission and every alternate outcome. The cockpit is inspired by Orion's but built from scratch, and it shows only systems the simulator really models. The map, the 3D view, Mission Control and the guided tutorial all show the same flight.

Factors considered during development:

The flight is modeled in a single plane and ends at atmospheric entry, and these simplifications are documented. Every constant cites its source, and when NASA documents contradict each other, the most recent one is used. Results don't depend on frame rate or simulation speed. The app uses no NASA logos and states that it is not affiliated with NASA.

NASA online resources used:

The data comes from the SLS Reference Guide for Artemis II, the Artemis II Reference Guide, the Artemis II Overview Timeline, Mission Availability, and Priorities and Objectives. The Moon's position in April 2026 comes from JPL Horizons, the entry angle from NASA paper AAS 24‑174, and the program cost from NASA OIG report IG‑22‑003. The app also links to the Artemis II press kit, the SLS gallery and "How to Fly NASA's Orion Spacecraft".
